**[CLIENT ADVISORY MEMORANDUM]{.underline}**

**Summary of Dutch AP Enforcement Decision No. AP-2025-0042 (TalentScope B.V.)**

*English-Language Summary and Analysis*

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

**Prepared by:**

> **Margaux Leclerc**, Partner Valcourt Deschênes LLP Rue de la Loi 227, 1040 Brussels, Belgium m.leclerc@valcourtdeschenes.eu

**Prepared for:**

> **Aisling Brennan**, Deputy General Counsel NovaBridge Technologies, Inc. abrennan@novabridge.com
>
> **Tomás Herrera-Vidal**, Chief Privacy Officer / Data Protection Officer NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. therrera@novabridge.eu

**Date:** January 20, 2025

**Reference:** This memorandum relates to EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 on Automated Processing of Employee Data in the Workplace Context (adopted December 12, 2024). A companion memorandum analyzing those guidelines in detail is being transmitted concurrently.

**Classification:** Privileged and Confidential --- Attorney-Client Communication / Attorney Work Product. Not for distribution outside of the NovaBridge Technologies legal and compliance teams without prior consultation with Valcourt Deschênes LLP.

**[1. Executive Summary]{.underline}**

On **January 15, 2025**, the **Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP)** --- the Dutch Data Protection Authority --- published **Decision No. AP-2025-0042**, imposing an administrative fine of **€8.5 million** on **TalentScope B.V.**, a Dutch *besloten vennootschap* operating a SaaS-based workforce analytics platform serving enterprise clients across the European Union. The fine represents approximately **2.8% of TalentScope\'s annual worldwide turnover of €303.6 million** for its most recently completed fiscal year.

The decision addresses four distinct GDPR violations identified in the course of an investigation that began in April 2024:

> 1\. **Inappropriate legal basis** for the continuous collection of employee productivity metrics, where TalentScope\'s controller-clients relied on legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) --- a legal basis the AP found inadequate in the employment context;
>
> 2\. **Failure to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)** specifically addressing TalentScope\'s predictive employee scoring features (sentiment analysis, burnout risk, and flight risk prediction), in violation of Article 35;
>
> 3\. **Excessive data retention** of raw employee survey data and productivity metrics for 30 months, which the AP found violated the storage limitation principle under Article 5(1)(e); and
>
> 4\. **Inadequate Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA)** for cross-border transfers of pseudonymized employee data to the United States for the purpose of ML model training, in violation of Article 46(1).

A particularly noteworthy feature of this decision is the AP\'s extensive reliance on the **EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 on Automated Processing of Employee Data in the Workplace Context** as interpretive authority, notwithstanding that the AP\'s investigation commenced in April 2024 --- well before the guidelines were formally adopted on December 12, 2024. The AP treated the guidelines as reflecting the correct interpretation of existing GDPR provisions rather than creating new legal obligations. This signals that supervisory authorities across the EU are likely to apply these guidelines to processing activities already underway, effectively foreclosing any argument that the guidelines represent \"new\" requirements subject to a grace period.

**This decision is directly relevant to NovaBridge Technologies.** PulseView\'s processing activities closely mirror TalentScope\'s sanctioned practices across multiple dimensions, including the legal basis for productivity metric collection, data retention periods, DPIA coverage, and cross-border transfer mechanisms. We highlight specific areas of concern and recommend priority actions in Section 6 and Section 7 below.

**[2. Background: The Investigation and TalentScope\'s Business]{.underline}**

**2.1 TalentScope B.V. --- Company Profile**

TalentScope B.V. is a Dutch *besloten vennootschap* (private limited liability company) headquartered in Amsterdam. The company operates a SaaS-based workforce analytics platform marketed to enterprise clients across the European Union and, to a lesser extent, in the United Kingdom and certain other jurisdictions. TalentScope\'s annual worldwide turnover for its most recently completed fiscal year was **€303.6 million**, placing it among the larger independent HR technology vendors in the European market.

TalentScope\'s platform collected and processed a broad range of employee data categories on behalf of its enterprise clients, including employee survey responses (engagement, satisfaction, and well-being surveys), productivity metrics (application usage statistics, meeting frequency and duration, email volume metadata, and calendar data), and AI/ML-derived analytical outputs. The platform generated predictive scores at the individual employee level, including employee sentiment scores, burnout risk indicators, and attrition predictions (commonly referred to as \"flight risk\" scores). These predictive outputs were generated using machine learning models trained on aggregated datasets and delivered to enterprise clients through dashboard interfaces, typically with a minimum cohort size to reduce re-identification risk in aggregated views.

In the context of its contractual relationships with enterprise clients, TalentScope operated as a **data processor** within the meaning of Article 4(8) GDPR. Enterprise clients --- the employers whose employees were the data subjects --- acted as data controllers. TalentScope\'s standard Data Processing Agreements reflected this processor/controller architecture.

The TalentScope platform is, in our assessment, **substantially similar** to NovaBridge\'s PulseView platform in terms of the categories of data processed, the nature of analytical outputs generated, the processor/controller architecture employed, and the cross-border transfer mechanisms utilized. This comparability underpins the relevance of the AP\'s decision to NovaBridge\'s compliance posture.

**2.2 Origin and Timeline of the Investigation**

The AP commenced its investigation of TalentScope in **April 2024**, acting on complaints received from employee works councils (*ondernemingsraden*) at two of TalentScope\'s Dutch enterprise clients. The complainant works councils alleged that employees had no meaningful ability to refuse participation in TalentScope\'s productivity monitoring and predictive scoring programs, and that employee data was being used in ways and for purposes not adequately disclosed to data subjects. The complaints specifically cited concerns about the generation of per-employee predictive scores (particularly flight risk predictions) and the lack of transparency regarding how those scores were used in workforce management decisions.

Upon receipt of these complaints, the AP initiated a formal investigation under Article 58(1) GDPR. The investigation expanded beyond the initially complained-of issues to encompass a comprehensive review of TalentScope\'s processing activities, including the legal basis relied upon for processing, TalentScope\'s DPIA practices, its data retention policies and schedules, and its mechanisms for cross-border data transfers, particularly transfers to the United States for the purpose of ML model training.

The AP issued a **preliminary findings report** to TalentScope in **September 2024**, detailing the tentative conclusions of the investigation and affording TalentScope the opportunity to respond. TalentScope submitted a written response and supplemental materials in October 2024. The AP considered TalentScope\'s submissions and published its **final decision on January 15, 2025**.

Notably, the **EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 on Automated Processing of Employee Data in the Workplace Context** were adopted by the European Data Protection Board on **December 12, 2024** --- approximately eight months after the AP\'s investigation commenced, three months after the AP issued its preliminary findings, and roughly five weeks before the AP published its final decision. The AP cited the guidelines extensively throughout its legal analysis. As discussed in Section 5 below, the AP characterized the guidelines as reflecting the correct interpretation of existing GDPR provisions rather than introducing new legal obligations, and stated that TalentScope could not credibly claim ignorance of the regulatory direction of travel, given that the EDPB had signaled its views on workplace monitoring through preliminary opinions and the publicly available draft guidelines from mid-2024 onward.

**[3. Violations Found]{.underline}**

**3.1 Violation 1: Inappropriate Legal Basis for Productivity Metric Collection (Article 6(1))**

**Finding.** TalentScope\'s enterprise clients relied on **legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR** as the legal basis for the continuous collection of employee productivity metrics, including application usage statistics, meeting frequency and duration data, and email volume metadata. TalentScope\'s standard Data Processing Agreements reflected this legal basis, identifying legitimate interest as the controller-client\'s stated Article 6(1) ground for the processing of productivity data.

The AP found that TalentScope\'s controller-clients had **not conducted a proper balancing test** as required under Article 6(1)(f). A valid reliance on legitimate interest requires the controller to demonstrate that its legitimate interests (or those of a third party) are not overridden by the fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject, taking into account the reasonable expectations of data subjects. The AP concluded that, given the specific characteristics of TalentScope\'s productivity monitoring, the controllers\' legitimate interests did not override the fundamental rights and freedoms of the affected employees. The AP cited three factors in reaching this conclusion:

> \(a\) **The systematic and semi-continuous nature of the data collection.** TalentScope\'s platform collected productivity metrics on an ongoing, near-real-time basis during working hours, creating a persistent monitoring environment rather than a time-limited or event-triggered data collection exercise.
>
> \(b\) **The inherent power imbalance in the employment relationship.** Employees were not in a position to meaningfully object to the processing without risking adverse consequences in the workplace. The AP emphasized that this power imbalance is a structural feature of the employment context that significantly weighs against the controller\'s interests in the balancing exercise.
>
> \(c\) **The reasonable expectations of employees.** The AP held that employees do not reasonably expect that granular data regarding their application usage, email metadata, and meeting participation will be continuously collected, aggregated, and analyzed to generate individual-level productivity profiles and predictive scores.

The AP cited **Paragraph 34 of the then-draft EDPB Guidelines 03/2024**, which states that legitimate interest is \"generally not an appropriate legal basis\" for systematic monitoring of employee productivity involving continuous or semi-continuous data collection. The AP treated this statement as an articulation of existing principles under the GDPR, not as a new regulatory requirement.

**Processor liability.** The AP acknowledged that TalentScope operated as a data processor, not as the data controller. However, the AP held that TalentScope had an independent obligation under the GDPR framework to ensure that its DPA templates, onboarding processes, and system design did not facilitate processing on an invalid legal basis. The AP emphasized that a processor cannot simply defer to the controller\'s asserted legal basis when the processor knows or should know that basis is inadequate --- particularly when, as in TalentScope\'s case, the processor designs the system architecture that dictates the nature and scope of processing. The AP observed that TalentScope\'s platform was specifically designed to collect the types and volumes of data for which legitimate interest was relied upon, and that TalentScope\'s standard DPA templates themselves identified legitimate interest as the applicable legal basis without providing for alternative bases or requiring controllers to document a balancing test.

**Penalty allocation.** This violation contributed to the overall administrative fine. The AP did not itemize per-violation fine amounts but identified this as one of the four bases for the €8.5 million total.

**Recommended alternative legal bases.** The AP indicated that appropriate alternatives to legitimate interest in this context include: (a) processing pursuant to collective agreements within the meaning of national implementations of Article 6(1)(b) or 6(1)(e) GDPR (in the Netherlands, this would include works council agreements under the *Wet op de ondernemingsraden* (Works Councils Act)); or (b) explicit, freely given consent meeting the heightened voluntariness requirements outlined in the EDPB Guidelines, which require that consent in the employment context be supported by safeguards ensuring no adverse consequences for employees who decline to participate.

**NovaBridge parallel.** NovaBridge\'s Data Processing Agreements with its enterprise clients cite Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest as the legal basis for processing productivity metrics in a manner that is materially identical to TalentScope\'s approach. This violation is therefore directly on point. We address the specific implications for NovaBridge in Section 6.1 below.

**3.2 Violation 2: Failure to Conduct a DPIA for Predictive Employee Scoring (Article 35)**

**Finding.** TalentScope deployed its predictive employee scoring features --- including employee sentiment analysis, burnout risk prediction, and flight risk (attrition) prediction --- **without first completing a Data Protection Impact Assessment** as required by Article 35 GDPR.

Article 35(1) requires a DPIA where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. The AP found that TalentScope\'s predictive scoring features met **at least two criteria** on the EDPB\'s non-exhaustive list of processing operations requiring a DPIA (as set out in the EDPB\'s Guidelines on DPIAs, WP 248 rev.01):

> \(a\) **Evaluation or scoring**, including profiling and predicting, especially from aspects concerning the data subject\'s performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences or interests, reliability, or behaviour. The AP found that TalentScope\'s generation of per-employee sentiment, burnout, and attrition scores clearly constitutes evaluation or scoring involving profiling and prediction related to workplace performance and well-being.
>
> \(b\) **Processing of data concerning vulnerable data subjects.** The AP classified employees as vulnerable data subjects within the meaning of the EDPB\'s DPIA guidelines, by reason of the structural power imbalance inherent in the employment relationship, which limits employees\' ability to consent to or refuse processing.

The AP further noted that a **third criterion** was arguably met: **systematic monitoring** of data subjects, given TalentScope\'s continuous collection of productivity metrics that fed into the predictive scoring algorithms.

**Insufficiency of the platform-level DPIA.** TalentScope argued that it had conducted a general platform-level DPIA covering the TalentScope analytics platform as a whole. The AP found this **insufficient**. The AP held that the platform-level DPIA did not specifically analyze the predictive scoring feature as a distinct processing activity with its own risk profile. In particular, the existing DPIA failed to address: (i) the per-employee nature of the scoring (as distinct from the delivery of aggregated outputs to clients), (ii) the risks specific to profiling within the meaning of Article 4(4) GDPR, or (iii) the potential applicability of protections against automated decision-making under Article 22 GDPR.

The AP emphasized that DPIAs must be **feature-specific** when new processing activities with distinct risk profiles are introduced. A platform-level assessment conducted at the time of initial product launch does not relieve the controller or processor of the obligation to reassess when significant new features --- particularly features involving profiling and predictive analytics --- are deployed. The DPIA must address the specific risks associated with the specific processing activity, not merely the general privacy posture of the platform.

**Relevance of Article 22.** The AP further noted, citing **Paragraph 58 of the draft EDPB Guidelines 03/2024**, that the generation of per-employee predictive scores constitutes profiling within the meaning of Article 4(4) and potentially triggers the protections of Article 22 GDPR (which restricts decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal effects or similarly significant effects on data subjects). The AP held that this is the case **regardless of whether the scores are ultimately delivered to clients in aggregated form**. The act of generating and retaining per-employee scores is itself the processing that falls within Article 22\'s scope, and the subsequent aggregation for reporting purposes does not retroactively neutralize the Article 22 implications of the per-employee processing that precedes it.

**Implications for NovaBridge.** NovaBridge\'s PulseView DPIA was last updated in **September 2023**. In light of this decision\'s emphasis on feature-specific DPIAs and the Article 22 analysis, we recommend that NovaBridge assess whether its existing DPIA is similarly insufficient. We address this further in Section 6.5 below.

**3.3 Violation 3: Excessive Data Retention (Article 5(1)(e))**

**Finding.** TalentScope retained raw employee survey data and productivity metrics for **30 months** from the date of collection. The AP found that this retention period violated the **storage limitation principle under Article 5(1)(e) GDPR**, which requires that personal data be kept in a form permitting identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the data is processed.

**TalentScope\'s justifications.** TalentScope advanced two principal justifications for the 30-month retention period:

> *First*, TalentScope argued that 30 months of raw data retention was necessary to enable year-over-year trend analysis for its enterprise clients. TalentScope asserted that at least two full years of historical data (plus an additional buffer period for analytical processing) were required to generate meaningful longitudinal insights into workforce trends.
>
> *Second*, TalentScope argued that the raw data was needed to maintain a sufficient volume of training data for its ML models, which were periodically retrained using historical datasets to improve predictive accuracy.

**The AP\'s analysis.** The AP rejected both justifications.

On the **trend analysis** justification, the AP found that aggregated or properly anonymized data could serve the purpose of year-over-year trend analysis and that retention of raw personal data was not necessary for this purpose. The AP acknowledged that trend analysis is a legitimate business objective but held that the principle of data minimization requires controllers and processors to achieve that objective using the least privacy-intrusive means available. Where aggregated data can serve the analytical purpose, retention of granular, identifiable (or re-identifiable) personal data is disproportionate.

On the **ML model training** justification, the AP held --- citing **Paragraph 71 of the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024** --- that model training constitutes a **separate processing purpose** from the provision of workforce analytics insights to controller-clients. Accordingly, retention of personal data for model training purposes cannot be justified by reference to the original collection purpose (i.e., providing analytics to clients). If a controller or processor wishes to retain personal data specifically for model training, it must identify a separate legal basis and articulate a separate retention justification for that purpose. The AP found that TalentScope had not done so.

Based on this analysis, the AP concluded that **12 months** of raw data retention was sufficient for the stated primary purpose of providing workforce analytics insights to controller-clients, and that TalentScope had not demonstrated a necessity for retention of raw personal data beyond that period.

The AP also noted that TalentScope\'s indefinite retention of aggregated and anonymized reports was **not problematic**, because truly anonymized data --- where the process of anonymization is irreversible and re-identification is not reasonably likely --- falls outside the material scope of the GDPR entirely.

**Key quotation from the decision** (translated from the Dutch original): *\"The principle of storage limitation requires controllers and processors to critically evaluate whether personal data remains necessary for the purposes for which it was collected. A general assertion that \'more data improves analytics\' does not constitute a valid justification under Article 5(1)(e). Where the stated purpose can be achieved with 12 months of data, retention of raw personal data for 30 months is manifestly excessive.\"*

**NovaBridge parallel.** NovaBridge retains raw survey data for **36 months** and productivity metrics for **24 months**. Both of these retention periods exceed TalentScope\'s sanctioned 30-month period, and significantly exceed the AP\'s 12-month benchmark. We address the specific implications in Section 6.2 below. We also note, for completeness, that NovaBridge\'s indefinite retention of aggregated and anonymized reports does not raise a data retention concern under the GDPR, consistent with the AP\'s analysis.

**3.4 Violation 4: Inadequate Transfer Impact Assessment for Model Training Transfers (Article 46(1))**

**Finding.** TalentScope transferred pseudonymized employee data from its EU processing environment to servers located in the United States for the purpose of global ML model training and improvement. These transfers were conducted under **Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)** adopted pursuant to the European Commission\'s Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021.

The AP found that TalentScope had conducted a general-purpose Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) covering its primary data processing activities, but had **not prepared a standalone, purpose-specific TIA** for the model-training transfer. The AP held that this was insufficient to satisfy the obligations under Article 46(1) GDPR, as interpreted in the *Schrems II* framework and subsequent EDPB guidance.

**The AP\'s reasoning.** The AP\'s analysis rested on the principle that the adequacy and effectiveness of supplementary measures and transfer safeguards must be assessed in relation to the specific processing purpose for which data is transferred. Citing **Paragraph 83 of the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024**, the AP held that where employee data is transferred to a third country for a **distinct processing purpose** (such as ML model training, as opposed to the primary analytics service), the risks associated with that specific purpose must be separately assessed. A general-purpose TIA --- even one that is comprehensive in its coverage of the primary processing activity --- does not adequately address the distinct risk profile of a different processing purpose carried out in a third-country environment.

The AP identified several respects in which the model-training transfer presents a different risk profile than TalentScope\'s primary analytics processing:

> \(a\) **Different processing operations.** Model training involves the ingestion of personal data into training pipelines, potential de-pseudonymization risks arising from the combination of training datasets, and storage in infrastructure environments that may differ from the primary production environment in terms of access controls and security posture.
>
> \(b\) **Different risk of government access.** The transfer of data to US-based infrastructure for model training purposes may implicate different surveillance risks than the primary processing, depending on the nature of the data involved, the identity of the recipient entity, and the applicability of US foreign intelligence surveillance authorities, including FISA Section 702.
>
> \(c\) **Different supplementary measures.** The supplementary measures appropriate for model training (such as differential privacy techniques, federated learning approaches, or enhanced pseudonymization specifically designed for training pipelines) may differ from those appropriate for the primary analytics service.

The AP acknowledged that pseudonymization is a relevant supplementary measure under the EDPB\'s Recommendations 01/2020 on supplementary measures but held that pseudonymization alone was **not sufficient to eliminate the need for a purpose-specific TIA**. The effectiveness of pseudonymization as a safeguard must itself be assessed in the context of the specific transfer, considering factors such as the likelihood of re-identification and the risk that the pseudonymization could be reversed by the data importer or a government authority in the receiving country.

The AP further noted that TalentScope\'s general TIA was approximately **18 months old** at the time of the investigation and had not been reviewed or updated since its initial completion, despite changes in the regulatory and geopolitical landscape that could affect the assessment of risks in the receiving country.

Finally, the AP included a **brief observation** that the SCC module selection should reflect the actual roles of the parties for the specific transfer purpose, noting that the relationship between the EU data exporter and the US-based entity receiving data for model training may differ from the relationship that governs the primary analytics processing. The AP did not elaborate on this point in detail but flagged it as an additional area of concern.

**NovaBridge parallel.** NovaBridge transfers pseudonymized EU data to Austin, Texas for ML model training under SCCs, supported by a general-purpose TIA completed in **March 2023**. We address the specific implications, including the need for a purpose-specific TIA and the AP\'s observation regarding SCC module selection, in Section 6.3 below.

**[4. Fine Calculation Methodology]{.underline}**

content.content:
AP imposed a total administrative fine of **€8.5 million** under **Article 83 GDPR**. The following summarizes the AP\'s approach to calculating the fine and the aggravating and mitigating factors considered.

**Turnover basis.** TalentScope B.V.\'s annual worldwide turnover for the most recently completed fiscal year was **€303.6 million**. This figure was used as the reference turnover for purposes of determining the statutory maximum fine.

**Statutory maximum.** Under Article 83(5) GDPR, the maximum administrative fine for the most serious categories of violations (including violations of Articles 5, 6, and Chapter V transfer provisions) is the higher of €20 million or **4% of total annual worldwide turnover** in the preceding business year. For TalentScope, the 4% threshold yields: €303.6 million × 4% = **€12.144 million**, which exceeds the €20 million alternative. Accordingly, the statutory maximum fine applicable to TalentScope was €12.144 million.

**Fine as percentage of statutory maximum and turnover.** The imposed fine of €8.5 million represents approximately **70% of the statutory maximum** (€8.5M ÷ €12.144M ≈ 70%) and approximately **2.8% of TalentScope\'s annual worldwide turnover** (€8.5M ÷ €303.6M ≈ 2.8%).

**Aggravating factors.** The AP cited the following aggravating factors in determining the quantum of the fine:

> • The processing affected a **large number of data subjects**. The AP did not disclose the precise number but described it as \"several hundred thousand employees\" whose data was processed through TalentScope\'s platform on behalf of its enterprise clients.
>
> • The violations were **ongoing and had not been remediated** at the time of the final decision. TalentScope had not modified its legal basis approach, conducted a feature-specific DPIA, adjusted its retention periods, or prepared a purpose-specific TIA during the course of the investigation.
>
> • TalentScope had been **informed of data protection concerns** by employee works councils prior to the AP\'s investigation. The works councils had raised concerns directly with TalentScope and with its enterprise clients, but TalentScope had not taken meaningful corrective action in response.
>
> • The **nature of the data** involved processing of employee data in an employment context, which the AP characterized as involving vulnerable data subjects by reason of the inherent power imbalance between employers and employees.

**Mitigating factors.** The AP credited the following mitigating factors:

> • TalentScope **cooperated with the AP** throughout the investigation, providing requested documentation and responding to inquiries in a timely manner.
>
> • TalentScope had implemented **certain privacy safeguards**, including pseudonymization of data in transit and at rest, and minimum cohort sizes for aggregated analytical outputs delivered to clients (designed to reduce the risk of re-identification of individual employees in aggregated reports).
>
> • There was **no evidence** that the violations had resulted in direct, quantifiable harm to individual data subjects. The AP acknowledged that the risks were primarily structural and systemic rather than tied to specific instances of identified harm.

**Collective assessment.** The AP did not itemize the fine by individual violation. Instead, the AP stated that all four violations were considered collectively in arriving at the total €8.5 million amount, taking into account their cumulative severity, the aggravating and mitigating factors, and the need for the fine to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive within the meaning of Article 83(1) GDPR.

**Application to NovaBridge.** The TalentScope fine methodology provides a useful benchmark for estimating NovaBridge\'s potential financial exposure. NovaBridge Technologies, Inc. reported global revenue of **\$312 million** for FY 2024, which translates to approximately **€289.4 million** at the current exchange rate of \$1.00 = €0.928. Applying the same 2.8% rate that the AP applied to TalentScope\'s turnover, a comparable fine for NovaBridge would be approximately **€8.103 million** (€289.4M × 0.028). The GDPR statutory maximum for NovaBridge, at 4% of turnover, would be approximately **€11.576 million** (€289.4M × 0.04).

NovaBridge\'s cyber insurance policy, underwritten by **Albion Specialty Insurance Ltd.**, carries a GDPR administrative fine sub-limit of **€5 million**. If NovaBridge were to face a fine comparable in magnitude to TalentScope\'s, the potential **uninsured exposure** would be approximately **€3.103 million** (€8.103M − €5M). This gap warrants immediate attention. We address the implications further in Section 6.4 below.

**[5. The AP\'s Use of the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024]{.underline}**

A noteworthy procedural and substantive feature of Decision No. AP-2025-0042 is the AP\'s extensive reliance on the **EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 on Automated Processing of Employee Data in the Workplace Context** as interpretive authority throughout the legal analysis.

**Timeline.** The AP\'s investigation of TalentScope commenced in **April 2024**. The EDPB Guidelines were in public consultation draft form during much of the investigation period and were formally adopted by the European Data Protection Board on **December 12, 2024**. The AP published its final decision approximately five weeks later, on **January 15, 2025**. The AP cited specific paragraphs of the guidelines --- including Paragraphs 34, 58, 71, and 83 --- as integral elements of its legal reasoning in connection with each of the four identified violations.

**The AP\'s stated justification.** The AP was explicit in its characterization of the guidelines\' legal status. The AP stated that the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 reflect the EDPB\'s interpretation of **existing provisions of the GDPR** --- specifically, Articles 5, 6, 22, 35, and 46 --- rather than creating new legal obligations. In the AP\'s view, the guidelines articulate principles that have been inherent in the GDPR since its entry into application in May 2018, and the EDPB\'s formal adoption of the guidelines simply provides a consolidated, authoritative restatement of those principles in the specific context of automated employee data processing. Accordingly, the AP treated the guidelines as persuasive interpretive authority and not as retroactively applied new law.

**Implications for regulated entities.** This approach carries significant consequences for companies operating in the workforce analytics space. It means that companies **cannot credibly argue** that they lacked notice of the regulatory expectations set out in the guidelines, or that the guidelines represent new requirements to which a grace period or transitional allowance should apply. The AP noted that TalentScope could not have been unaware of the general regulatory trajectory regarding workplace monitoring, given that the EDPB had published preliminary opinions and consultation drafts on the topic from mid-2024 onward, and that data protection concerns regarding employee productivity monitoring had been the subject of regulatory commentary for several years prior.

**Broader enforcement signal.** In our assessment, the AP\'s approach in this decision is likely to be followed by other national supervisory authorities across the EU. The EDPB Guidelines are adopted by consensus of the member state supervisory authorities, and while they are not legally binding in the same way as a regulation, they carry substantial persuasive weight and reflect the shared regulatory position of the supervisory authorities that enforce the GDPR. Companies should treat the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 as effectively in force and should not delay compliance adjustments while awaiting national-level implementation or further elaboration.

For NovaBridge, this means that the compliance gaps identified in this memorandum --- and those to be addressed in our companion EDPB Guidelines advisory --- should be treated as matters of current urgency rather than future planning. The regulatory expectations articulated in the guidelines are, in the AP\'s view, already the law.

**[6. Implications for NovaBridge Technologies]{.underline}**

This section draws specific parallels between TalentScope\'s sanctioned practices and NovaBridge\'s current operations. It is intended to highlight the most salient areas of risk and to recommend further internal review. Additional implications arising from the EDPB Guidelines themselves (as distinct from the TalentScope enforcement decision) will be addressed in our companion memorandum.

**6.1 Legal Basis for Productivity Metrics**

NovaBridge\'s Data Processing Agreements with its **740+ enterprise clients** cite **Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest** as the legal basis for the processing of productivity metrics collected through the PulseView platform. This is materially identical to the legal basis relied upon by TalentScope\'s controller-clients, which the AP found inadequate in Decision No. AP-2025-0042.

In light of this decision, NovaBridge should **urgently review** its reliance on legitimate interest as the stated legal basis in its DPAs and in its controller-client onboarding processes. The AP\'s finding that a processor bears responsibility for facilitating processing on an invalid legal basis --- particularly where the processor designs the system architecture that dictates the scope of processing --- is directly applicable to NovaBridge\'s position.

Transitioning to an alternative legal basis will require NovaBridge to work with its controller-clients to identify and implement appropriate alternatives, which may include collective agreements (works council agreements or similar instruments under applicable national law) or consent mechanisms meeting the heightened voluntariness requirements set out in the EDPB Guidelines (Paragraph 47). This transition will necessitate amendments to all existing DPAs and will likely require updates to the privacy notices provided by controller-clients to their employees. Given that NovaBridge has **over 740 enterprise client DPAs** to amend, this represents a significant operational undertaking. We recommend that NovaBridge initiate a legal basis transition project promptly, beginning with the identification of the highest-risk client relationships (e.g., Dutch clients, clients in jurisdictions with active supervisory authorities, and clients with organized works councils).

**6.2 Data Retention**

NovaBridge currently retains raw survey data for **36 months** and productivity metrics for **24 months**. For reference, TalentScope was fined for retaining raw data for **30 months**, and the AP established a benchmark of **12 months** as a sufficient and proportionate retention period for raw personal data collected for the purpose of providing workforce analytics insights.

NovaBridge\'s retention periods **exceed** TalentScope\'s sanctioned periods on both measures. The 36-month raw survey data retention period, in particular, is significantly longer than TalentScope\'s 30-month period that the AP found manifestly excessive. This creates an elevated compliance risk for NovaBridge in the event of a supervisory authority investigation.

We recommend that NovaBridge conduct a thorough, documented retention necessity assessment, evaluating for each data category whether the current retention period is strictly necessary and proportionate for the stated primary processing purpose. Any retention beyond 12 months should be supported by specific, documented justification demonstrating why the shorter period is insufficient. NovaBridge should also separately assess whether any data is retained for the secondary purpose of ML model training and, if so, whether a separate legal basis and separate retention justification exist for that purpose, consistent with the AP\'s finding that model training constitutes a distinct processing purpose.

We note, for completeness, that NovaBridge\'s indefinite retention of aggregated and anonymized reports does not raise a data retention concern under the GDPR, as truly anonymized data falls outside the regulation\'s material scope. This is consistent with the AP\'s treatment of TalentScope\'s anonymized reporting outputs.

**6.3 Transfer Impact Assessment**

NovaBridge transfers pseudonymized EU employee data to Austin, Texas for ML model training under Standard Contractual Clauses, supported by a general-purpose Transfer Impact Assessment completed in **March 2023**. This arrangement is structurally analogous to TalentScope\'s sanctioned transfer, and the AP\'s reasoning applies directly.

The TalentScope decision confirms that a **standalone, purpose-specific TIA** is required for transfers of personal data to a third country for the purpose of ML model training. NovaBridge\'s current TIA is a general-purpose assessment that does not specifically address the model-training transfer as a distinct processing activity with its own risk profile. This gap places NovaBridge in the same position as TalentScope with respect to this violation.

Additionally, NovaBridge\'s TIA is now nearly **two years old** (completed March 2023) and has not been reviewed or updated since its initial completion. Even apart from the purpose-specificity issue, the failure to periodically review and update the TIA is itself a compliance concern, particularly given changes in the US legal landscape and the adoption of the EDPB Guidelines in the intervening period.

We recommend that NovaBridge prepare a **supplemental or entirely new TIA** specifically addressing the transfer of pseudonymized EU employee data to Austin for ML model training. This TIA should assess the specific risks associated with the model-training transfer, including: (a) the risk of de-pseudonymization in the training pipeline environment; (b) the potential applicability of US government access authorities, including FISA Section 702, to data held in the Austin infrastructure; (c) the effectiveness of pseudonymization and any other supplementary measures in the specific context of model training; and (d) the legal and practical ability of the US-based recipient to comply with its obligations under the SCCs.

We also note that the AP\'s decision included a **brief reference to the importance of correct SCC module selection** reflecting the actual roles of the parties for the specific transfer purpose. The AP flagged that the relationship between the EU data exporter and the US entity receiving data for model training may differ from the contractual relationship governing the primary processing, potentially requiring a different SCC module than the one currently in place. We flag this observation for further analysis in our separate EDPB Guidelines advisory memorandum, as a detailed assessment of SCC module applicability requires examination of the specific contractual architecture between NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. and its US parent entity.

**6.4 Financial Exposure**

Applying the TalentScope fine methodology to NovaBridge\'s financial profile yields the following exposure estimates:

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Metric**                         **TalentScope**         **NovaBridge (Estimated)**
  ---------------------------------- ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------
  Annual worldwide turnover          €303.6M                 \$312M / **€289.4M** (at \$1.00 = €0.928)

  Fine at 2.8% of turnover           €8.5M                   **€8.103M**

  GDPR statutory maximum (4%)        €12.144M                **€11.576M**

  Cyber insurance GDPR sub-limit     N/A                     **€5.0M** (Albion Specialty Insurance Ltd.)

  **Potential uninsured exposure**   N/A                     **€3.103M**
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

These figures are illustrative and based on the assumption that a supervisory authority would apply a comparable rate of turnover to NovaBridge\'s case. Actual fines are determined on a case-by-case basis considering the specific facts and circumstances, including the aggravating and mitigating factors described in Section 4. However, the TalentScope precedent provides a credible benchmark for financial planning purposes.

We recommend that NovaBridge take the following steps in light of this financial exposure:

> \(a\) **Insurance review.** Explore increasing the GDPR fine sub-limit with Albion Specialty Insurance Ltd. or in the broader insurance market. The current €5 million sub-limit is materially below the estimated exposure range.
>
> \(b\) **Board and audit committee briefing.** Ensure that the board audit committee and NovaBridge\'s securities counsel (**Kessler Whitmore LLP**) are briefed on the identified GDPR compliance gaps and the potential financial exposure. GDPR enforcement risk is a material risk factor that may require disclosure in NovaBridge\'s S-1 registration statement in connection with the **Q3 2025 IPO timeline**. Failure to disclose a known material risk could itself create securities liability.
>
> \(c\) **Financial planning.** Factor the potential uninsured exposure of approximately €3.103 million into NovaBridge\'s financial planning, reserve considerations, and risk management framework.

**6.5 Additional Observations**

The TalentScope decision\'s emphasis on DPIA adequacy should prompt NovaBridge to **review its existing PulseView DPIA**, which was last updated in **September 2023**. The AP\'s finding that a platform-level DPIA is insufficient when distinct processing features (such as predictive scoring) carry their own risk profiles raises the question of whether NovaBridge\'s current DPIA adequately covers PulseView\'s full range of processing activities.

In particular, the DPIA should be assessed for whether it adequately addresses:

> \(a\) The **per-employee nature of sentiment scoring** in the context of Article 22 GDPR and automated decision-making protections. The AP\'s analysis in the TalentScope decision (and the EDPB\'s position at Paragraph 58 of the Guidelines) makes clear that per-employee score generation constitutes profiling that potentially triggers Article 22, regardless of whether scores are delivered to clients in aggregated form.
>
> \(b\) The **separate processing purpose of model-training transfers** and the specific risks associated with that processing, which the current DPIA may not address.
>
> \(c\) The new interpretive guidance provided by the **EDPB Guidelines 03/2024**, which were not available at the time of NovaBridge\'s September 2023 DPIA update.

Given the number and significance of the areas requiring reassessment, we recommend a **comprehensive DPIA refresh** rather than a piecemeal update. This refresh should be conducted with reference to both this enforcement decision and the EDPB Guidelines, and should involve a fresh assessment of risks, supplementary measures, and the necessity and proportionality of each processing activity.

We will address the EDPB Guidelines in greater detail --- including the consent mechanism requirements, Article 22 implications for per-employee scoring, and the separate legal basis question for model training --- in our companion advisory memorandum: *\"EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 --- Summary and Analysis\"* (transmitted concurrently).

**[7. Key Takeaways and Recommended Next Steps]{.underline}**

Based on the foregoing analysis, we recommend the following priority actions for NovaBridge Technologies:

1\. **Legal Basis Review (Urgent).** Initiate an immediate review of NovaBridge\'s reliance on Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest in all Data Processing Agreements governing the collection and processing of productivity metrics through the PulseView platform. Develop a transition plan for moving to an alternative legal basis (collective agreements or consent with robust voluntariness safeguards) across NovaBridge\'s **740+ enterprise client relationships**. Prioritize Dutch clients and clients in jurisdictions with active supervisory authorities. This review should include an assessment of the DPA template language and controller-client onboarding processes to ensure NovaBridge does not continue to facilitate processing on an invalid legal basis.

2\. **Retention Period Review (High Priority).** Conduct a formal, documented retention necessity assessment for all categories of personal data processed through PulseView. NovaBridge\'s current retention periods --- **36 months** for raw survey data and **24 months** for productivity metrics --- both significantly exceed the AP\'s 12-month benchmark and exceed TalentScope\'s sanctioned 30-month period. Be prepared to justify any retention beyond 12 months with specific, documented rationale demonstrating necessity and proportionality. Separately assess whether any personal data is retained for the purpose of ML model training and, if so, whether a separate legal basis and retention justification exist.

3\. **Purpose-Specific TIA (High Priority).** Commission a new or supplemental Transfer Impact Assessment specifically addressing the transfer of pseudonymized EU employee data to Austin, Texas for ML model training. This TIA should be a standalone assessment addressing the specific risks of the model-training transfer, including de-pseudonymization risk, US government access risk (FISA Section 702), and the effectiveness of supplementary measures in the model-training context. The existing March 2023 general-purpose TIA should also be reviewed and updated.

4\. **DPIA Refresh (High Priority).** Initiate a comprehensive update to the PulseView Data Protection Impact Assessment, incorporating the interpretive guidance from the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 and the enforcement precedent from Decision No. AP-2025-0042. The refreshed DPIA should specifically address the per-employee predictive scoring features, Article 22 implications, the model-training transfer, and the updated regulatory framework.

5\. **Insurance Coverage Review.** Engage with **Albion Specialty Insurance Ltd.** to explore increasing the GDPR administrative fine sub-limit beyond the current **€5 million** level. Given the estimated potential exposure of approximately **€8.103 million** and the resulting **€3.103 million** uninsured gap, the current coverage level is inadequate relative to the identified risk.

6\. **IPO Coordination.** Brief **Kessler Whitmore LLP** (securities counsel) and the NovaBridge board audit committee on the identified GDPR compliance gaps and their potential impact on S-1 risk factor disclosures and the **Q3 2025 IPO timeline**. GDPR enforcement risk, including the potential for a multi-million euro fine and the existence of known compliance gaps, may constitute a material risk requiring affirmative disclosure in the registration statement. Failure to disclose such risk could create separate securities liability.

7\. **Monitor Appeals.** Monitor whether TalentScope B.V. appeals the AP\'s decision to the competent Dutch administrative court. An appeal could alter the precedential weight of certain aspects of the decision, though it would not diminish the immediate compliance urgency given the AP\'s demonstrated willingness to enforce these standards and the EDPB\'s formal adoption of the underlying guidelines.

We note that additional recommendations regarding the consent mechanism for productivity monitoring, Article 22 protections for per-employee scoring, and the legal basis for model-training data processing will be provided in our companion advisory memorandum on the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024. The two memoranda should be read together, and we recommend scheduling a joint call with the NovaBridge legal and compliance teams to discuss prioritization and implementation planning.

**[8. Disclaimer and Limitations]{.underline}**

This memorandum is based on the published text of AP Decision No. AP-2025-0042 (TalentScope B.V.), dated January 15, 2025, and publicly available information regarding TalentScope B.V. and its workforce analytics platform. All translations from the Dutch original are our own and are provided for convenience; in the event of any discrepancy, the Dutch-language text of the decision as published by the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens controls.

This summary and analysis is provided for informational purposes to NovaBridge Technologies, Inc. and NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. and constitutes legal advice protected by attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. It should not be shared outside the NovaBridge Technologies legal and compliance teams, or with any third party, without prior consultation with Valcourt Deschênes LLP. Unauthorized disclosure may result in a waiver of privilege.

The AP\'s decision may be subject to appeal by TalentScope B.V. The analysis herein reflects the current state of the law and regulatory guidance as of January 20, 2025, and may require revision in light of subsequent developments, including any appellate proceedings, further guidance from the AP or the EDPB, or changes in relevant law.

For a detailed analysis of the EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 referenced throughout this decision, and for additional recommendations concerning consent mechanisms, Article 22 compliance, and the legal basis for model-training data processing, please see our companion memorandum: **\"EDPB Guidelines 03/2024 on Automated Processing of Employee Data in the Workplace Context --- Summary and Analysis\"** (transmitted concurrently under separate cover).

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

For questions regarding this memorandum, please contact the undersigned or your primary relationship contact at Valcourt Deschênes LLP.

**Margaux Leclerc** Partner Valcourt Deschênes LLP Rue de la Loi 227, 1040 Brussels, Belgium m.leclerc@valcourtdeschenes.eu +32 2 XXX XX XX

**[NOVABRIDGE TECHNOLOGIES EU B.V.]{.underline}**

**[Internal Memorandum --- Data Processing Description]{.underline}**

**[NovaBridge PulseView Data Processing Overview]{.underline}**

**Date:** January 10, 2025

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **To:**                             **Aisling Brennan, Deputy General Counsel; Raina Chaudhary, VP of Engineering; Privacy & Compliance Team**
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **From:**                           Tomás Herrera-Vidal, Chief Privacy Officer / Data Protection Officer, NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V.

  **Email:**                          therrera@novabridge.eu

  **Re:**                             PulseView Platform --- Data Processing Activities Description

  **Classification:**                 Confidential --- Internal Use Only

  **Version:**                        3.1
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Purpose of This Document**

This memorandum documents and describes NovaBridge\'s current data processing activities for the PulseView platform as they pertain to EU/EEA personal data. It covers all processing categories, the legal bases upon which such processing relies, the applicable retention schedules, the consent mechanisms deployed for sentiment analysis processing, the cross-border data transfer arrangements between NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. and NovaBridge Technologies, Inc., and the current status of the Data Protection Impact Assessment. This document serves as the primary internal reference for NovaBridge\'s GDPR compliance posture with respect to the PulseView platform and should be treated as a living document subject to periodic revision as regulatory developments, operational changes, or supervisory authority guidance warrant updates.

Right-click to update Table of Contents

**[1. Introduction and Scope]{.underline}**

NovaBridge Technologies, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered at 4200 Congress Avenue, Suite 1100, Austin, TX 78701, United States. The company completed its Series D funding round in 2023, having raised a cumulative total of approximately \$185 million to date across all financing rounds. As of the date of this memorandum, NovaBridge employs approximately 1,400 individuals globally across offices in the United States, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Singapore. For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, NovaBridge reported global revenue of approximately \$312 million.

NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. is a Dutch *besloten vennootschap* (private limited liability company) registered at Herengracht 482, 1017 CB Amsterdam, Netherlands (KvK Registration No. 82471923). NovaBridge EU serves as the company\'s EU subsidiary and is the entity through which all EU/EEA-facing operations are conducted. NovaBridge EU is the entity subject to GDPR oversight and is the establishment through which the company\'s data processing activities relating to EU/EEA personal data are directed and managed. Under the GDPR\'s one-stop-shop mechanism established by Articles 56 and 60, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch Data Protection Authority, serves as the lead supervisory authority for NovaBridge EU.

PulseView is NovaBridge\'s proprietary SaaS workforce analytics and employee engagement platform. The platform enables enterprise clients to administer employee engagement surveys, collect and analyze workforce productivity metrics, and generate sentiment analysis insights --- including burnout risk indicators and attrition/flight risk predictions --- for their employee populations. PulseView is NovaBridge\'s core commercial product and the source of substantially all of the company\'s recurring subscription revenue.

This document describes all processing activities involving EU/EEA personal data conducted through the PulseView platform, encompassing the collection, storage, analysis, and cross-border transfer of such data. As of the date of this memorandum, NovaBridge EU processes the personal data of approximately 3.2 million EU-based data subjects. These data subjects are employees of NovaBridge\'s enterprise clients who are enrolled in the PulseView platform by their respective employers. NovaBridge currently serves over 740 enterprise clients with EU/EEA-based employee populations. EU/EEA revenue for FY 2024 was approximately \$94 million, representing 30.1% of global revenue.

Tomás Herrera-Vidal serves as Chief Privacy Officer and Data Protection Officer for NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V., appointed pursuant to Article 37 of the GDPR. Mr. Herrera-Vidal holds IAPP certifications including the Certified Information Privacy Professional/Europe (CIPP/E) and the Certified Information Privacy Manager (CIPM). In his capacity as DPO, Mr. Herrera-Vidal reports on a dotted-line basis to Aisling Brennan, Deputy General Counsel of NovaBridge Technologies, Inc., and has direct access to the board of directors of NovaBridge EU.

NovaBridge EU has engaged Margaux Leclerc, Partner at Valcourt Deschênes LLP, Rue de la Loi 227, 1040 Brussels, Belgium (m.leclerc@valcourtdeschenes.eu), as outside EU data protection counsel. Ms. Leclerc advises on regulatory interpretation, supervisory authority engagement, enforcement defense, and cross-border transfer compliance matters.

**[2. Data Processing Activities]{.underline}**

**2.1 Overview of Processing Role**

NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. processes EU personal data in its capacity as a **data processor** on behalf of its enterprise clients, who serve as the **data controllers** in accordance with Article 28 of the GDPR. The enterprise clients determine the purposes and means of the processing of their employees\' personal data through the PulseView platform; NovaBridge processes such data only on behalf of and in accordance with the documented instructions of these controllers.

Standard Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) are executed and in place with all 740+ EU enterprise clients. These DPAs are based on NovaBridge\'s standard template, which has been in use since the platform\'s EU launch and is periodically updated for regulatory changes. Each DPA explicitly defines the enterprise client as the data controller and NovaBridge Technologies EU B.V. as the data processor for all categories of processing described in this memorandum.

The DPAs describe the subject matter and purpose of processing broadly, encompassing the three processing categories set out in Sections 2.2 through 2.4 below. Importantly, the DPAs apply the processor designation uniformly across all processing activities, including the collection and analysis of survey responses, the ingestion and processing of productivity metrics, the generation of sentiment analysis outputs, and any ancillary activities undertaken in support of service provision. The DPAs do not distinguish between processing roles for different processing purposes. Specifically, the scope of processing described in the DPAs refers to the overall \"provision of workforce analytics services\" and does not carve out or separately characterize any individual processing purpose --- including the use of pseudonymized data for machine learning model training and improvement --- as a distinct processing activity with its own purpose limitation, legal basis, or role allocation. All processing activities are addressed under a single processor designation and a single overarching purpose statement.

**2.2 Category 1: Employee Survey Responses**

**Description.** NovaBridge collects and processes employee engagement survey responses submitted through the PulseView platform. Surveys are configured by the enterprise client (the controller) and may include both free-text open-ended questions and Likert-scale rating questions. Topics covered by surveys typically include employee satisfaction, workplace culture, managerial effectiveness, work-life balance, and organizational alignment.

**Volume.** Approximately 18.7 million individual survey responses are collected annually from EU-based data subjects across all enterprise clients.

**Data Types.** The personal data elements collected in connection with survey responses include: textual free-form answers to open-ended questions; numerical scale ratings for Likert-scale questions; timestamps recording the date and time of survey submission; and employee pseudonymous identifiers assigned by the PulseView platform to associate responses with individual employees without exposing direct identifiers.

**Collection Method.** Employees access the PulseView platform using employer-provided credentials (typically via single sign-on integration with the enterprise client\'s identity provider). Once authenticated, employees complete surveys within the PulseView interface. Surveys are administered on a periodic basis as scheduled by the enterprise client, typically quarterly or semi-annually.

**Legal Basis.** The legal basis cited in the DPAs for the processing of employee survey responses is the **legitimate interest of the controller under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR**. The DPAs state that the controller\'s legitimate interest is \"understanding workforce engagement levels and improving employee experience.\" This legal basis is applied uniformly across all enterprise clients and is documented in the standard DPA template.

**Storage Location.** All raw survey response data for EU-based data subjects is stored in the AWS eu-central-1 region (Frankfurt, Germany).

**Retention Period.** Raw survey responses are retained for **36 months** from the date of collection. Upon expiration of the retention period, data is removed through an automated purge job as described in Section 4 below.

**2.3 Category 2: Productivity Metrics**

**Description.** NovaBridge collects and processes aggregated application usage statistics, meeting frequency and duration data, and email volume metadata for employees enrolled in the PulseView platform. It is important to note that email content is not collected --- only volumetric and frequency metadata (e.g., the number of emails sent and received per day) is ingested. Similarly, the content of meetings, calendar entries, or collaboration tool communications is not accessed; only structural metadata such as meeting count, average duration, and collaboration tool activity frequency is processed.

**Collection Method.** Productivity metrics are collected via API integrations with the enterprise client\'s deployed productivity suites, including calendar systems, email platforms, and collaboration tools. These integrations are configured by the enterprise client\'s IT administrators in coordination with NovaBridge\'s implementation team. Data is ingested via scheduled API calls on a daily cadence for all enrolled employees. The collection is continuous and semi-continuous in nature --- once an employee is enrolled, productivity metrics are ingested automatically each day without requiring any affirmative action by the employee.

**Data Types.** The personal data elements processed in connection with productivity metrics include: application usage hours per day (broken down by application category); number of meetings attended per day and average meeting duration; email send and receive counts per day; collaboration tool activity metrics (e.g., number of messages posted, files shared, or comments made in collaborative workspaces); employee pseudonymous identifiers; and timestamps for all data points.

**Legal Basis.** The legal basis cited in the DPAs for the processing of productivity metrics is the **legitimate interest of the controller under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR**. The DPAs state that the controller\'s legitimate interest is \"monitoring workforce productivity trends and identifying operational inefficiencies.\" The DPAs include a brief balancing-test summary stating that productivity metrics are collected at an aggregated and statistical level and that individual employees are not singled out for adverse performance action solely on the basis of these metrics. The balancing-test summary further states that the processing is proportionate to the legitimate interest pursued, given the pseudonymized nature of the data and the aggregated reporting format. However, the balancing-test language in the DPAs was drafted at the time of the platform\'s initial EU launch and has not been revisited, updated, or refreshed since that time.

**Storage Location.** All raw productivity metric data for EU-based data subjects is stored in the AWS eu-central-1 region (Frankfurt, Germany).

**Retention Period.** Raw productivity metrics are retained for **24 months** from the date of collection. Upon expiration of the retention period, data is removed through an automated purge job as described in Section 4 below.

**2.4 Category 3: Sentiment Analysis Outputs**

**Description.** NovaBridge generates machine-learning-derived outputs for employees enrolled in the PulseView platform, including: (a) sentiment scores reflecting an overall assessment of employee engagement sentiment, (b) burnout risk indicators assessing the likelihood that an employee is experiencing or approaching burnout, and (c) \"flight risk\" predictions estimating the probability that an employee may voluntarily leave the organization within a defined time horizon. These outputs are collectively referred to as \"sentiment analysis outputs.\"

**Input Data.** Sentiment analysis outputs are generated from a combination of employee survey responses (Category 1) and productivity metrics (Category 2) using NovaBridge\'s proprietary machine learning models. The models are trained on historical data from across NovaBridge\'s global client base and are applied to individual employee data to generate per-employee predictions and scores.

**Per-Employee Score Generation.** Scores are computed on a **per-employee basis**. Each individual employee enrolled in the sentiment analysis module receives a sentiment score, a burnout risk indicator, and a flight risk prediction. These per-employee scores are generated by the ML models and stored in the NovaBridge database associated with the employee\'s pseudonymous identifier. The per-employee scores constitute the primary output of the ML inference pipeline and are the basis from which all downstream reporting is derived.

**Delivery to Clients.** Sentiment analysis outputs are delivered to enterprise clients **exclusively in aggregated cohort reports** with a minimum cohort size of five (5) employees. Individual employee scores are never directly shared with the enterprise client. Cohort reports present aggregated sentiment scores, burnout risk distributions, and flight risk trends at the team, department, or organizational unit level, depending on the client\'s reporting configuration.

However, the **per-employee scores are generated, stored, and retained** in NovaBridge\'s systems for the full retention period, irrespective of whether they are ever surfaced in a client-facing report. The per-employee scores persist in the NovaBridge database and are available for use in historical trend computations, model validation activities, and internal quality assurance processes. The fact that only aggregated outputs are delivered to clients does not alter the fact that per-employee scores are created and maintained at the individual level within NovaBridge\'s infrastructure.

**Legal Basis.** The legal basis cited in the DPAs for the processing of sentiment analysis outputs is the **explicit consent of data subjects under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR**, obtained through an in-platform consent flow described in Section 3 below. The consent-based legal basis was selected at the time the sentiment analysis module was designed, in recognition of the sensitivity of the processing and the nature of the outputs generated.

**Storage Location.** All sentiment analysis output data for EU-based data subjects is stored in the AWS eu-central-1 region (Frankfurt, Germany).

**Retention Period.** Per-employee sentiment analysis outputs are retained for **18 months** from the date of generation. Upon expiration of the retention period, data is removed through an automated purge job as described in Section 4 below.

**Module Launch Date.** The sentiment analysis module was launched in Q3 2023. This launch occurred after the completion of the original Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for the PulseView platform, which was finalized in June 2022. The DPIA was subsequently updated in September 2023 to reflect the addition of the sentiment analysis module, as described in Section 6 below.

**[3. Consent Mechanism for Sentiment Analysis]{.underline}**

The consent mechanism for sentiment analysis processing was designed in mid-2023, in advance of the Q3 2023 launch of the sentiment analysis module. The design process was led by the product and engineering teams under the direction of Raina Chaudhary, VP of Engineering, in collaboration with the Privacy & Compliance team. The consent flow was implemented as a platform-level feature integrated into the PulseView user interface.

**Consent Flow Description.** When an employee first logs into the PulseView platform --- or upon first login after the sentiment analysis module was activated for that employee\'s enterprise client --- a **pop-up consent notice** is displayed. The consent notice appears as a modal overlay that must be addressed before the employee can proceed to any other functionality within the platform.

**Scope of Consent Notice.** The consent notice is presented on a **single screen** and covers **both** the employee\'s participation in engagement surveys administered through PulseView **and** the use of the employee\'s data for sentiment analysis purposes, including the generation of burnout risk indicators and flight risk predictions. The consent notice explains, in summary terms, the types of data that will be collected (survey responses and productivity metrics), the purposes for which data will be processed (engagement analysis, sentiment scoring, burnout and flight risk assessment), and the fact that aggregated reports will be provided to the employee\'s employer. The consent text does not separately describe the use of employee data for ML model training and improvement activities.

**Consent Action.** The consent notice presents a **single \"I Agree\" button** at the bottom of the screen. There is no separate opt-in or opt-out toggle that would allow an employee to consent to participation in engagement surveys while declining consent to sentiment analysis processing, or vice versa. The consent is bundled: an employee either consents to all described processing activities by clicking \"I Agree,\" or consents to none of them.

**Consequence of Declining Consent.** Employees who decline consent --- by closing the pop-up window, navigating away, or otherwise not clicking the \"I Agree\" button --- **cannot access the PulseView survey platform at all**. Employees who decline are redirected to a screen displaying the following message: *\"You must accept the data processing terms to use PulseView. Please contact your IT administrator if you have questions.\"* No alternative survey participation mechanism is offered to employees who do not consent. Employees who decline consent are effectively excluded from the engagement survey process administered through PulseView.

**Consent Withdrawal.** There is no documented mechanism for employees to withdraw consent after initial acceptance. The PulseView platform does not present a consent management dashboard, a preference center, or a withdrawal option within the employee\'s account settings. No documented process exists for employees to request consent withdrawal via email, support ticket, or any other channel. The DPAs do not specify an obligation on NovaBridge to facilitate consent withdrawal requests from individual data subjects, nor do they describe a process by which controllers would relay such requests to NovaBridge.

**Consent Acceptance Rate.** Approximately **97.3%** of employees who are presented with the consent screen click \"I Agree\" and proceed to use the platform. This acceptance rate has remained consistent since the sentiment analysis module was launched.

**[4. Data Retention Schedule]{.underline}**

The table below summarizes the retention periods applicable to each category of EU personal data processed through the PulseView platform:

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Data Category**                                  **Retention Period**   **Measured From**    **Deletion Method**
  -------------------------------------------------- ---------------------- -------------------- ----------------------------
  Employee survey responses (raw)                    36 months              Date of collection   Automated purge job

  Productivity metrics (raw)                         24 months              Date of collection   Automated purge job

  Sentiment analysis outputs (per-employee scores)   18 months              Date of generation   Automated purge job

  Aggregated/anonymized cohort reports               Indefinite             N/A                  Not scheduled for deletion
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Retention periods for survey responses and productivity metrics were established at the time of the PulseView platform\'s EU launch. The retention period for sentiment analysis outputs was established at the time the sentiment analysis module was launched in Q3 2023. These retention periods were set based on internal product team assessments of the volume of historical data required for three primary operational needs: (a) trend analysis for client-facing reporting, which benefits from multi-year historical baselines; (b) machine learning model training and validation, which requires large and temporally diverse datasets to maintain model accuracy; and (c) troubleshooting, audit, and quality assurance purposes, which require access to historical data in the event of client inquiries or system anomalies.

The retention periods have **not been formally reviewed or justified through a storage limitation analysis under Article 5(1)(e) GDPR** since their initial establishment. No separate assessment has been conducted to determine whether the retention periods remain proportionate to the purposes for which the data is processed, or whether shorter retention periods would be sufficient to meet the stated operational nee
